They had sent these representatives to Adrian, whom they had chosen as arbitrator. Traveling from Paris to Calais through empty towns and deserted countryside, the deputies had nourished a fierce hatred of one another, and now argued their respective cases with undiminished partisan zeal.

By questioning them separately and pursuing a lengthy inquiry, we discovered the actual condition of affairs in Paris. Ever since parliament appointed him Ryland’s deputy, every surviving English person had accepted Adrian’s authority. He was the captain who would guide us from our native country into unfamiliar lands, our legislator and protector. When our emigration was first planned, we had envisaged no lasting division of our company; the authority governing the entire body rose by degrees to its highest point in the Earl of Windsor. Unforeseen events, however, altered those plans and separated most of our people from their supreme leader for almost two months. They had crossed in two separate parties, and disagreements began between them upon reaching Paris.

They found Paris deserted. When the plague first appeared, returning merchants and travelers, together with correspondence, kept us regularly informed of the disease’s devastation on the continent. As the deaths increased, that intercourse dwindled and finally stopped. Even within England, communication between different parts of the island grew infrequent and slow. No ship crossed the waters between Dover and Calais. If some sorrowful traveler sailed from France to learn whether his relatives among us lived or died, the hungry sea would often engulf his little vessel; or, after a day or two, he caught the sickness and died before relating the story of France’s desolation. Thus we remained largely ignorant of continental conditions and still entertained a faint hope of finding many companions across its broad expanse. Yet the forces that had reduced England so terribly had found even wider opportunity for destruction in the neighboring country. France was empty. Not a single person appeared along the whole road between Calais and Paris. In Paris a few remained, perhaps a hundred, resigned to their approaching fate. They wandered the capital’s streets and gathered to speak of earlier days with the liveliness, and even gaiety, that rarely abandons the people of this nation.

The English occupied Paris without opposition. Its lofty houses and confined streets were without life. A few pale figures could be seen at their customary meeting place in the Tuileries. They wondered why the islanders would come to their doomed city, for in the extremity of misery sufferers always believe their own share of a calamity the most bitter. So, when we endure intense pain, we would willingly exchange the particular torment that makes us writhe for another afflicting some different portion of the body.

“Shall I call on them? Or on Miss Bates? She is nearer still. And I am not sure Miss Bates would not understand the wishes of the others as well as anybody. I believe we need a larger council. What if I went to ask Miss Bates to join us?”

“Well, if you wish,” Mrs. Weston replied with some hesitation, “if you believe she can be useful.”

“You will learn nothing relevant from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She will be nothing but gratitude and delight, and give you no information. She will not even hear your questions. I can see no benefit in asking Miss Bates’s advice.”

“But she is so entertaining, so very entertaining! I am exceedingly fond of listening to her. And there is no need to bring the entire family, you know.”

At this point Mr. Weston joined them, heard the suggestion, and heartily approved it.

“Yes, do, Frank. Fetch Miss Bates, and let us settle the business immediately. I am certain she will enjoy the plan, and I know no one better suited to showing us how to overcome difficulties. Bring Miss Bates. We are becoming rather too particular. She is a continual example of how to be happy. But bring both of them. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady—?”

“The old lady! No, naturally I mean the young one. I shall consider you a great dunce, Frank, if you fetch the aunt and leave the niece.”

“Oh, forgive me, sir. I did not think of her at once. Certainly, if that is your wish, I shall try to persuade both of them.” And off he ran.

Well before he returned escorting the small, tidy, briskly moving aunt and her graceful niece, Mrs. Weston, being a good-natured woman and an excellent wife, had inspected the passage once more. She discovered its defects to be far less serious than she had first imagined—indeed, quite insignificant—and this ended their difficulties in deciding. Everything else, in theory at least, went perfectly smoothly. The lesser arrangements of chairs and tables, music and lighting, supper and tea, seemed to settle themselves, or were put aside as trifles that Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes could resolve whenever convenient. Everyone invited would surely attend. Frank had already written to Enscombe suggesting a stay a few days beyond his fortnight, a request that could not possibly be denied. It was to be a delightful dance.

When Miss Bates arrived, she agreed with the utmost warmth that it must be so. They no longer needed her as an adviser, but as an approver—a much safer role—she was thoroughly welcome. Her praise, embracing the whole and every detail, enthusiastic and unceasing, inevitably pleased them. For another half-hour they walked back and forth through the rooms, some making suggestions, others listening, all happily anticipating what lay ahead.

Sydney Carton stopped in the street, still uncertain where to turn. “At Tellson’s banking-house at nine,” he said thoughtfully. “Would it be wise to let myself be seen meanwhile? I believe it would. These people ought to know that someone like me is here; it is a prudent precaution and perhaps an essential preliminary. But caution, caution, caution! I must consider it fully.”

He checked his steps, which had begun to move toward a purpose, and paced a little along the street as darkness gathered, following his thought through to its possible results. His original judgment held. “It is best,” he said, his decision finally made, “that these people know there is such a man as myself here.” He then turned toward Saint Antoine.

That day Defarge had identified himself as a wine-shop keeper in the suburb of Saint Antoine. Someone familiar with the city could easily locate his house without making inquiries. Once he had established where it stood, Carton left those narrower streets, ate dinner at a place of refreshment, and afterward fell into a deep sleep. For the first time in many years, he took no strong liquor. Since the previous night he had drunk only a little weak, light wine; and the night before, he had slowly poured the brandy onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth, like a man finished with it.

It was already seven o’clock when he woke, rested, and returned to the streets. On his way toward Saint Antoine, he paused before a shop-window containing a mirror and made small adjustments to the untidiness of his loose cravat, coat collar, and unruly hair. Then he proceeded straight to Defarge’s and entered.

The shop contained only one customer: Jacques Three, with his restless fingers and croaking voice. Carton had seen him on the Jury. He stood at the small counter, drinking and talking with Defarge and his wife. The Vengeance joined in their conversation as though she were a regular member of the establishment.

Carton came in, sat down, and requested a small measure of wine in very poor French. Madame Defarge glanced at him indifferently, then more closely, then more sharply still, before approaching him herself to ask what he had ordered.

He repeated his request.

“English?” Madame Defarge asked, lifting her dark eyebrows with curiosity.

He looked at her as though even the sound of a single French word took time to convey its meaning to him. Then he replied in the same pronounced foreign accent.
